title: Stop after about 3 failed fixes, then reset or escalate
summary: After about three failed attempts to fix the same problem, stop the agent and either restart with a clearer task or hand it to a person. Later attempts rarely succeed and cost the most.
signals: Agent sessions with more than 3 attempts at the same failing check
Spend on sessions that end without an accepted change
Tasks escalated to a person after the cap

title: Loop only against a check the machine runs
summary: Only let an agent retry when a test, build or linter decides whether the attempt worked. Retries judged by the model itself mostly repeat the same mistake.
signals: Agent sessions that end with no test, build or lint run in the log
Tasks the agent called done that fail CI on first push
Retries per task rising while pass rate stays flat

title: Loops driven by self-critique alone
summary: Don't let an agent improve its work by reviewing itself with no outside check. It tends to approve its own wrong answers; give it a test or a linter to loop against instead.
signals: Agent sessions that loop with no test, build or lint step
Changes the agent marked correct that fail CI or review

title: Keep each agent's context small
summary: Keep each agent's working context short: clear or compact old steps, and split long tasks across fresh sessions. Agents work better when old observations stop crowding the context.
signals: Context size per step in long sessions
Sessions that hit the context limit
Mistakes late in long sessions that early steps got right

title: Work in small batches with strong version control
summary: Keep agent changes small and merge them often, with every step committed so it can be reverted. Small batches keep AI speed from turning into delivery instability.
signals: Lines changed per merged PR, trending up
Change failure rate as AI use grows
Reverts that undo more than one logical change

title: Sandbox anything unattended
summary: Run any agent that works without a person watching inside a sandbox, with no access to secrets or production. Once permission prompts are off, the sandbox is the only boundary.
signals: Unattended runs with permission prompts disabled outside a sandbox
Agents that can read private data, take untrusted input and send data out

title: Manage cost with visibility and friction
summary: Make agent spend visible per team and per task, set sensible default effort levels, and nudge before large spends. Route simple tasks to cheaper models, but check that results hold up.
signals: Agent spend per merged change, by team
Sessions over a spend threshold each week
Accepted-change rate after routing tasks to cheaper models

title: Check the agent more often on risky code
summary: Check the agent after every step when you are unsure or the code is risky, such as auth and payments, and let it run several tasks when you are confident. Try this for a sprint.
signals: Defects found after release in auth and payment code
Review time per PR, by risk level

title: Log steps to the first human correction
summary: Record how many steps agents take before a person has to correct them. This shows how long you can leave an agent alone on your codebase.
signals: Steps before the first human correction, per session
Sessions corrected only after 20 or more steps

title: Compare fresh and continued context per iteration
summary: Test whether your loops do better starting fresh each iteration or continuing the same session. Run the same backlog items both ways.
signals: Agent spend per merged change, fresh versus continued
Accepted-change rate, fresh versus continued

title: Run low-risk tickets unattended overnight
summary: Batch a few low-risk tickets for agents to work on unattended, gated by checks that are cheap, run often and are hard to fake. Review the results the next morning.
signals: Overnight PRs mergeable without changes
Minutes of fix-up per overnight PR

title: Keep a machine-readable done list
summary: For a feature spread across sessions, keep a list of steps where only a passing check can mark a step done. It stops the agent from declaring the feature finished early.
signals: Steps marked done that fail review or CI
Premature completion claims caught by the list

title: Align on product, architecture and design before code
summary: Agree on what to build, the architecture and the design with a person before agents write code. Try it on a few features and skip it on comparable ones.
signals: Rework per feature, with and without upfront alignment
Review rounds per PR

title: Run checks inside the agent session
summary: Give agents lint, type-check and test commands to run before they open a PR, so problems are fixed in the session instead of in review. Start with one repo.
signals: Problems found in review that a session check would have caught
Failing CI runs on agent PRs' first push

title: Time-track agent work by phase
summary: For a month, log how agent work time splits between defining the task, waiting, reviewing and fixing up. It shows where the real bottleneck moved.
signals: Share of time defining tasks
Share of time reviewing
Share of time fixing up agent output

title: Track agent outcomes on novel versus boilerplate work
summary: Tag tickets as boilerplate, port or novel and track how agent work turns out for each. Agents tend to help most on repetitive work and least on new design.
signals: Agent PRs mergeable without changes, by ticket type
Fix-up time per PR, by ticket type
Reverts, by ticket type

title: Add a minimum-effort floor to an agent's exit condition
summary: Require an agent to spend a minimum time or number of steps before it can give up on a task. Try it on one agent for two weeks.
signals: Tasks the agent abandons early
Tasks completed after the floor is added

title: Compare a capped retry loop with a stronger model at equal cost
summary: Test whether a cheaper model with a capped test-and-retry loop beats a stronger model in one pass at the same spend. Use the same tests for both.
signals: Accepted-change rate, cheap-loop versus strong model
Spend per accepted change for each

title: Let a cheaper model execute a strong model's plan
summary: Have a strong model write and a person approve the plan, then let a cheaper model carry it out. Compare with a strong model doing both on comparable tickets.
signals: Review rounds per PR, by executor model
Rework per ticket, by executor model
Spend per merged change

title: Keep a growing regression list in long-running loops
summary: In multi-day agent work, require a test for each finished step and run them all before starting the next. Long loops tend to break work that was already done.
signals: Earlier steps broken by later steps
Finished steps with no test protecting them

title: Pick among several agent attempts
summary: On a few tickets, run several agent attempts and pick the best using test results and one reviewer. Check whether the gain is worth the extra spend.
signals: Mergeable-as-is rate, best-of-several versus single attempt
Spend per merged change

title: Run a strong model's checks once as a final gate
summary: With a strong model, try running the full checks once at the end instead of after every step. Compare on comparable tickets.
signals: Accepted-change rate, final gate versus per-step checks
Tokens and minutes per accepted change

title: Fix the harness before the code
summary: When an agent gets something wrong, first change the spec, check or guidance that let it through, then fix the code. Try it for a month.
signals: The same kind of agent defect recurring each month
Time spent changing checks and guidance

title: Try a local mid-size model on small pre-planned tasks
summary: Try a model running on your own hardware for small, well-specified changes and scripts. Compare with the hosted model on the same tickets and tests.
signals: Test pass rate, local versus hosted
Minutes and cost per ticket

title: Have scheduled agents file reports, not PRs
summary: Let scheduled agents file short reports, such as one per newly flaky test, instead of opening PRs. Keep the volume low enough that people read them.
signals: Reports that lead to a merged fix
Minutes per week spent reading agent reports
Duplicate or ignored reports

title: Measure time to an accepted change, not lines or PRs
summary: Measure each task by time to an accepted, merged change, and fix that outcome before you start measuring. Lines, PRs and tokens can rise while delivery stalls, and the same tool can look faster or slower depending on the measure.
signals: Time from task start to accepted, merged change
Lines or PR counts rising while time to merge stays flat
Merged changes reworked within 30 days

title: Time real tasks instead of trusting forecasts or surveys
summary: Judge whether agents speed the team up by timing real tasks, not by forecasts or surveys. Predictions of speedup are often wrong even in direction, and self-reports shift with how you ask and who answers.
signals: Gap between forecast and timed duration per task
Speedup claimed in retros or surveys that timed tasks don't confirm
Survey answers that change with question wording or respondent role

title: Grade agents on tests they never saw
summary: Judge agent patches by human merge review or by tests the agent never saw, not by the suite it worked against. Weak checks let suspicious patches through, and passing the repo's own tests doesn't make an agent PR mergeable.
signals: Agent PRs green on CI that reviewers reject or send back
Patches passing visible tests but failing held-back tests
Passing agent patches reviewers flag as suspicious

title: Normalise cost by accepted output
summary: Try tracking cost per accepted change, not per request or the total bill, on one team for a quarter. A tool that looks cheaper per request can cost more per result.
signals: Cost per accepted change next to cost per request, per model
Months where the bill rises but cost per accepted change falls
Turns per task on a cheaper model against its list-price saving
Model or tool choices that change when ranked by cost per accepted change

title: Ranking people by AI usage
summary: Don't rank or set targets for people by how much they use AI; track merged, used changes instead. Usage measures activity, not value, and usage targets get gamed.
signals: Usage climbing while merged changes per person stay flat
Self-prompting loops or other activity run only to raise usage
Agent sessions that produce no commit or PR

title: Randomise real tickets to test speed gains
summary: Randomly assign about 30 real tickets to AI-allowed or not, and record each developer's time forecast before they start. Self-reported time savings are unreliable, so compare forecasts with what was actually timed.
signals: Time to merge, AI-allowed versus not, against each forecast
Rework within 30 days, AI-allowed versus not
Whether AI-allowed tickets merge faster without more rework

title: Report confidence intervals on model comparisons
summary: For the next two model comparisons, report the paired difference on the same tasks with a confidence interval, not just which scored higher. A small score gap between models is often read as a real difference when it isn't.
signals: Share of model "wins" whose interval excludes zero
Model switches made on a gap that sits inside the interval

title: Check LLM judges against human labels
summary: Have two engineers label about 100 agent traces and compare their verdicts with an LLM judge from a different model family before you rely on the judge. Claims that a well-prompted judge is reliable enough rarely come with agreement data.
signals: Agreement rate between engineers and the judge on labelled traces
Judge verdicts that flip when the agent retries until it passes
Traces the judge passes that the engineers fail

title: Run a production-trace review loop
summary: On one LLM feature for a quarter, sample 5-10% of production traces, review them weekly and turn failures into eval cases. Keep the loop if it catches failures your offline evals miss.
signals: Failures first found in trace review versus in offline evals
Eval cases added from reviewed traces per week
Incidents on the feature that neither review nor evals caught

title: Test whether a hidden test set changes agent behaviour
summary: Split one internal eval into visible and hidden tests, and run the agent with and without telling it a hidden set exists. Evidence that this pushes agents toward more general code is thin, so check it on your own tasks.
signals: Gap between visible and hidden pass rates, told versus not told
Agent changes that special-case visible test inputs

title: Rerun past tickets before each model upgrade
summary: Before each model upgrade, rerun a fixed set of past tickets on the old and new model and compare cost as well as results. A newer model is not always better, and it can cost more.
signals: Accepted-change rate on the ticket set, old versus new, with interval
Cost per accepted change, old versus new model
Model upgrades rolled out without a rerun

title: Show cost per merged change next to total spend
summary: For a quarter, put cost per merged change, including review and correction time, next to total spend on one dashboard. Read cost per run rather than the bill, and keep the view if it changes a decision.
signals: Cost per merged PR and per review, including correction time
Months where spend rose but cost per merged change fell
Budget or tooling decisions that differ from reading the bill alone

title: Compare token spend with merged output before setting usage targets
summary: Before setting any usage target, compare each team's token spend with its merged changes for a quarter, without publishing a ranking. Usage leaderboards get gamed, and spend may not track output.
signals: Token spend against merged changes per team, per month
Teams with rising spend and flat merged or used output

title: Declare effort and wanted review on AI-drafted artifacts
summary: For a month, have one team label AI-drafted artifacts with what it is, why it's sent and how much review is wanted. Low-quality AI work costs recipients hours, and nobody has measured whether labelling helps.
signals: Reviewer hours on low-quality AI work, before and after (self-report)
Review minutes per AI-drafted artifact
Share of AI-drafted artifacts sent with a label

title: Name AI-enabled deliverables in advance
summary: At the start of a quarter, list the deliverables you would only attempt with AI, then check at the end which shipped and are in use. Some gains show up as extra scope, not speed.
signals: Share of named deliverables shipped by quarter end
Shipped named deliverables actually in use

title: Count abandoned and rewritten agent changes
summary: For a month, count agent changes merged as-is, merged after rewrite and abandoned, and report all three next to the merge rate. Time-saved reports hide the effort spent evaluating and throwing away output.
signals: Share of agent changes abandoned or rewritten before merge
Review hours per merged agent change
Merge rate rising while the abandoned share also rises

title: Cross-score agents on task sets each one built
summary: Build one small internal task set with agent A and another with agent B, then score both agents on both sets. A task set built and checked with one agent may favour that agent.
signals: Score gap between the agent that built a set and the other
Tool choices that flip once agents are cross-scored

title: Track feature cycle time by PR type
summary: For a quarter, have an agent tag a quarter of PRs by type and compute doc-to-launch cycle time for features next to PR count. PR count misleads: PRs can get much bigger while their number stays flat.
signals: Feature share of PRs
Median doc-to-launch time for features
Whether feature cycle time moves with PR count

title: Compare spend tiers with quick approval against hard caps
summary: For a quarter, put one team on spend tiers with quick manager approval and per-session spend shown, and another on a hard cap. Hard caps are common but easy to get around.
signals: Spend per merged change on each team
Requests to move up a tier
Work blocked or worked around under the cap

title: Write context files by hand and keep them short
summary: Write the repo's context file yourself and keep it short: build commands, conventions and the few rules the agent keeps breaking. A short file saves time and tokens; a long one mostly adds cost.
signals: Context file length growing month over month
Agent tokens per task before and after each edit to the file
Rules in the file the agent still breaks in review

title: LLM-generated context files
summary: Don't let the agent write its own context file. Generated files restate what the agent can already read, so they raise cost without making tasks succeed more often.
signals: Context files committed by an agent without human edits
Agent spend per task rising after a context file change
Context file content that repeats the README or code

title: Keep context lean
summary: Give the agent only what the task needs: the relevant files, not the whole repo or every doc. Agents miss facts more often as context grows.
signals: Tokens loaded per agent task, by repo
Agent answers that miss a fact already in its context
Sessions that hit the context limit or auto-compact

title: Trim tools and what they return
summary: Expose a few tools with short descriptions, cap how much each returns, and batch repeated calls into one script. Every tool description and long result costs context the agent needs for the task.
signals: Context taken by tool and MCP descriptions at session start
Tool results over a few hundred lines landing in context
Same tool called many times in a row in session logs

title: Tools shaped for people, not agents
summary: Don't hand the agent tools built for human navigation, like paged search or whole-file viewers. Agents do better with narrow tools that return a small, relevant slice.
signals: Session steps spent paging through tool output
Whole files read when only a function was needed
Agent tasks stalling inside one tool loop

title: Commit a plan before code
summary: Have the agent write a plan, review it, and commit it before any code. Try it on comparable tickets for a month against prompting straight to code.
signals: Review rounds per PR, plan-first versus direct
Reverts within 30 days, plan-first versus direct
Time from ticket start to merge

title: Enforce the most-violated rules with hooks
summary: Take the three rules agents break most and enforce them with hooks or checks instead of context-file text. Try it in some repos and compare with repos that rely on the file alone.
signals: Rule violations per PR, hook repos versus file-only repos
Review comments that restate a rule already in the context file

title: Move repeated procedures into on-demand skills
summary: Move a procedure the agent repeats, like a release checklist, out of the always-loaded context file and into a skill that loads only when needed. Try it in half the repos.
signals: Tokens per session in repos with and without the skill
Tasks that need the procedure completed correctly

title: Add a focused commit or review subagent
summary: Add a small subagent whose only job is to check the change before commit or review. Run it for two weeks and see what it catches that the main agent missed.
signals: Problems the subagent flags before human review
Problems human reviewers still find that the subagent missed
Extra minutes and tokens per PR the subagent adds

title: Rephrase negative rules positively
summary: Rewrite "don't do X" rules in the context file as "do Y". Try it on five rules and compare how often they are broken before and after.
signals: Violations of each rewritten rule per PR, before and after

title: Prefer diverse few-shot examples over perfect labels
summary: When a prompt uses examples, cover the range of real cases rather than polishing a few. Compare example sets on one recurring generation task.
signals: Wrong outputs on a fixed set of real past cases, per example set
Output fixes needed per run

title: Split unknowns from assumptions in specs
summary: Add a section to the spec template that separates what is unknown from what is assumed, so the agent doesn't build on a guess. Use it on the next five features.
signals: Rework caused by a requirement found after coding started
Questions raised in review that the spec should have answered

title: Groom memory files monthly
summary: Once a month, have a person prune the context and memory files: remove stale rules and resolve contradictions. Agents don't clean up their own memory.
signals: Stale or contradictory rules found at each grooming
Context file size month over month
Agent mistakes traced to an outdated rule

title: Add a candour ground rule
summary: Tell the agent to say plainly when a request is flawed instead of just doing it. Test it with a handful of deliberately flawed requests, with and without the rule.
signals: Flawed requests the agent pushes back on
Flawed requests carried out without comment

title: Try autocomplete before agents for novel code
summary: For genuinely new code, try writing it with autocomplete before handing it to an agent; it can be faster to show intent in code than in prose. Alternate both for a month on novel modules.
signals: Rework per PR, autocomplete-first versus agent-first
Time to merge for novel modules
Review comments about not fitting codebase conventions

title: Have agents write scripts for deterministic work
summary: For counting, parsing or format conversion, have the agent write a script once and run the script, instead of asking the agent to do it each time. Scripts give the same answer every run.
signals: Errors in repeated deterministic tasks done by the agent directly
Tokens spent on tasks a script could do

title: Match spec rigour to how long the system lives
summary: Keep specs checked in CI for systems that will live for years, and use the lightest spec that removes ambiguity for short-lived ones. Try both on comparable features.
signals: Spec and code disagreeing when checked
Rework per feature
Defects found after release

title: Compare whole-module context with retrieval
summary: Test whether loading a whole module into context beats letting the agent search for what it needs. Ask the same set of questions about one repo both ways.
signals: Questions about the repo answered correctly, by method
Tokens per answer, by method

title: Keep one AGENTS.md and point other tool files at it
summary: Keep one context file, AGENTS.md, and make other tools' files point to it rather than copying rules into each. Compare a repo set up this way with one keeping copies in sync by hand.
signals: Rules that differ between tool-specific context files
Edits per month needed to keep context files in sync

title: Sort context into global, local and ambient
summary: Label context by scope: global rules for every repo, local rules for one repo, and ambient reference material. Review the global set monthly with one team.
signals: Stale or conflicting entries found at each review
Time to find the right context file for a change

title: Restart the session when output degrades
summary: When a session keeps getting worse after a few corrections, start a new one with a short summary of the goal and constraints instead of continuing.
signals: Turns from first prompt to an accepted result
Rules you re-state more than once in a session
Long sessions ending without an accepted change

title: Recover the spec after the first working version
summary: Try building a first working version, then writing the spec from it, instead of writing the spec first. Compare both on comparable features.
signals: Requirements discovered late, by approach
Rework per feature, by approach

title: Measure how much of an agent spec is code
summary: Check how much of a detailed agent spec is really pseudocode or formulas. If most of it is, writing the code may be cheaper than writing the spec.
signals: Share of a spec that is pseudocode, formulas or exact behaviour
Two agents building different behaviour from the same spec

title: Grant agent autonomy only on loosely defined work
summary: Let agents run with little supervision only where any reasonable result is fine, and supervise closely where the result must match exact requirements. Tag the next tickets and compare.
signals: Turns to an accepted result, loosely versus tightly defined tickets
Rework, loosely versus tightly defined tickets

title: Scale the spec workflow to the size of the problem
summary: Use a one-paragraph brief for small fixes and a written spec only for features. Heavy spec tools turn small bugs into long documents that take longer to review than the code.
signals: Minutes reviewing the spec against minutes reviewing the code
Review rounds per change, by spec size

title: Make the context file a short index over a docs directory
summary: Replace one long context file with a short index that points to topic files in a docs folder, plus linters for the rules that matter. Compare for a month.
signals: Rule violations caught in review, before and after the split
Agent time per task, before and after

title: Ground agents in a company context graph
summary: Give agents a searchable map of who owns which services, recent PRs and incidents, instead of only repo files. Test it on ownership and incident questions.
signals: Ownership and incident questions the agent answers correctly
Turns and tokens per answer

title: Call CLIs from skills instead of MCP tool lists
summary: Where an MCP server loads many tool descriptions into every session, have skills call the equivalent command-line tool instead. Compare on a few recurring tasks.
signals: Context taken by MCP tool descriptions per session
Task success, MCP versus CLI

title: Keep an accountable human review on AI changes
summary: Have a named human review and own every AI change before it merges. Agents generate code faster than it can safely ship, and changes that pass every test often still need fixing.
signals: AI changes merged without a human approver
Fix-up minutes on agent PRs that were already green
Incidents per merged PR, AI-authored vs human-authored

title: Send risky PRs to people, the rest to AI review
summary: For a month, label PRs by risk, send auth, schema, public API and similar changes to human reviewers, and give low-risk changes AI-only review. Teams report this works, but nobody has measured it.
signals: Merged PRs per week alongside change failure rate, by review route
Incidents traced to PRs labelled low risk
PRs whose risk label proved wrong in hindsight

title: Add an intake gate to the agent PR template
summary: In one repo, make the agent PR template require purpose, a size limit, test output and proof the change ran before review starts.
signals: Review rounds per agent PR, before vs after the gate
Agent PRs abandoned or closed unmerged
PRs sent back for missing template fields

title: Slice big agent branches for review
summary: Require agent branches over 400 lines to be split into stacked PRs of about 200 lines, each with one purpose. Small single-purpose PRs are easier to review properly.
signals: Review minutes per PR, sliced vs unsliced
Post-merge defects, sliced vs large agent PRs
Agent PRs over 400 lines merged without slicing

title: Review plans instead of diffs
summary: On 10 features, review the agent's plan, tests or schema for 5 and only the diff for the other 5. A short plan may be far cheaper to review than the code generated from it.
signals: Review minutes per feature, plan review vs diff-only
Post-merge defects per feature in each group

title: Run two AI reviewers in parallel
summary: Run two AI reviewers side by side on the same PRs for a month. Different AI reviewers tend to flag different problems, with little overlap.
signals: Valid findings that only one reviewer raised
Comments dismissed as noise, per reviewer

title: Show only high-confidence AI review comments
summary: For a month, show reviewers only high-confidence AI review comments, with duplicates merged. A flood of low-value comments trains people to approve without reading.
signals: Share of AI review comments acted on
PRs approved within minutes while AI comments are still open

title: Phase in deterministic gates
summary: In one repo, phase in boundary and duplicate-code rules: record a baseline, then warn on changed files, then block.
signals: Findings per PR at each phase
Findings dismissed as false positives
Warnings fixed before merge vs ignored

title: Write a review policy
summary: In one repo, adopt a REVIEW.md that sets review passes, severity levels and a cap on nits, and bars the writing agent from approving its own work.
signals: Nit comments per PR
Review minutes per PR, before vs after the policy
Agent PRs approved by the same agent that wrote them

title: Set explicit rejection criteria
summary: For a quarter in one team, reject green code the author can't explain and require hand-written commit messages.
signals: Reverts per month
Later changes that rework recently merged code
PRs rejected because the author couldn't explain them

title: Add a simplification pass before review
summary: In one repo, add an agent pass that asks "can this be simpler?" before human review. Without it, each bug tends to get its own patch.
signals: Lines changed per PR, with vs without the pass
Bugs per feature after merge

title: Try QA instead of line-by-line review on an internal tool
summary: On one internal tool, replace default line-by-line diff review with QA and fuzzing.
signals: Escaped defects on the tool vs before the trial
Hours on review vs QA per release

title: Match review depth to task uncertainty
summary: For a month, tag agent PRs as low or high uncertainty at planning: light inspection for bug fixes, deeper structural review for novel features.
signals: Escaped defects per uncertainty tag
Review minutes per PR, by tag
PRs whose uncertainty tag proved wrong in hindsight

title: Turn repeated review findings into agent skills
summary: For a month, turn every review comment seen twice into an agent skill or a lint rule instead of fixing it by hand. That stops the same mistake coming back in later PRs.
signals: Repeats of the same finding per 10 PRs
Skills or lint rules added from review comments

title: Set how much agent code is read by risk tolerance
summary: For a quarter, tag repos by risk tolerance: read generated code in full where mistakes cost money, safety or legal standing, and accept throwaway work by testing and running it.
signals: Escaped defects and incidents per risk tag
Review minutes per PR, by risk tag

title: Give reviewers time and authority to reject
summary: For a quarter, give reviewers of agent PRs a stated time budget and explicit authority to reject, and compare with a team that has neither. A reviewer who can only approve is there to take the blame.
signals: Agent PRs rejected or sent back
Escaped defects, trial team vs comparison team
Review minutes per agent PR

title: Check AI-approved PRs by running them
summary: On 10 AI-approved PRs, have an engineer run the change in a test environment and check it does what it claims. An AI review reports what the reviewer thinks, not what the system does.
signals: AI-approved PRs where running the change shows a missed defect
Engineer minutes per manual check

title: Cap AI review at three rounds
summary: For a month, cap AI review at three rounds in one repo, re-reviewing only the new diff each round, and leave a comparable repo uncapped. An agent reviewer and agent author can otherwise loop for dozens of rounds.
signals: Review rounds per PR to pass, capped vs uncapped
Escaped defects and reverts, capped vs uncapped

title: Score the AI reviewer on past incidents
summary: Collect 20 past revert or incident PRs and 20 known-clean PRs, and score the AI reviewer on them before each config change. Keep a change only if the score rises.
signals: Bugs caught on the incident set, per reviewer config
False alarms on the clean set, per reviewer config

title: Review a checked spec instead of the code
summary: On 10 configuration or infrastructure changes, approve a tool-checked list of what must and must not change, then read the code anyway and log what the list missed. The risk sits in what the list leaves open.
signals: Defects the list missed but code review caught
Minutes on the list vs minutes on the code
List items left vague or open

title: Give the AI reviewer repo access and test execution
summary: On the same 30 PRs, run the AI reviewer with only the diff and with repository access plus test execution, and compare. A reviewer that sees the whole repo and runs code may catch more with fewer false alarms.
signals: AI review comments that led to a code change, per setup
False alarms per PR, per setup
Defects found after merge on the 30 PRs

title: Enforce access and approvals outside the model
summary: Keep credentials in code, validate output formats in code, and check every tool call against a policy instead of trusting prompt instructions. A prompt can be talked out of a rule; a policy check can't. (OWASP LLM01, LLM06)
signals: Tool calls that run without a policy check
Credentials reachable from the agent's context or environment
Policy denials per week, and which tools trigger them

title: Remove one leg of the lethal trifecta
summary: Don't let one agent hold private data, untrusted content and a way to send data out at the same time, and require approval for anything that sends, spends or deletes. Approval limits the damage but doesn't remove the weakness. (OWASP LLM01, LLM02)
signals: Agents with private data, untrusted input and an outbound channel at once
Send, spend or delete actions run without human approval

title: Verify a package's publisher and registration date
summary: Treat agent installs as privileged: pin with hashes, scan the full dependency tree, and require human approval plus a publisher and registration-date check for any new package. Agents suggest packages that don't exist, and attackers register those names. (OWASP LLM09, LLM03)
signals: New packages added without human approval
Dependencies not pinned with hashes
New packages registered recently or with unknown publishers

title: Give security-sensitive changes a human review
summary: Don't let the writing agent approve its own PR, and give auth and payment changes a human security review. People trust assisted code more even when it is less secure; explicit instructions and function signatures in the prompt help. (OWASP LLM09)
signals: Agent PRs on auth or payment paths merged without a security review
Agent PRs approved by the agent that wrote them
Security findings per agent PR vs human PR

title: Keep people hands-on
summary: Protect time for people to write and debug code themselves, not only through an agent. Without it, people lose skill and understand less of the code they ship. (OWASP LLM09)
signals: Hours people spend coding and debugging without the agent
Reviewers who can't explain an agent's change when asked

title: Grant agents the fewest tools and the minimum scopes
summary: Give agents only the tools they need, avoid open-ended shell and fetch where possible, run tools with the user's minimum scopes, and authorise in downstream systems. Let agents act up to the production gate, never through it. (OWASP LLM06)
signals: Agent commits merged without review, as a share of agent commits
Agents with open-ended shell or fetch tools
Agent actions that passed the production gate

title: Deny secrets to agents and force the sandbox
summary: Block agent access to .env* and secrets/**, force the sandbox with a domain allowlist, and use short-lived scoped CI credentials and secret scanning. Never put credentials or controls in CLAUDE.md, rules or skills, since agents can be made to reveal them. (OWASP LLM02, LLM07)
signals: Agent reads of .env*, secrets/** or ~/.ssh in session logs
Secret-scanning hits on agent changes
Credentials or controls found in CLAUDE.md, rules or skills

title: Allowlist MCP servers and enforce access at the tool layer
summary: Allow only approved MCP servers, keep privileged tools apart from external ones, require fixed-schema responses, and confirm sensitive actions outside the model. A poisoned tool description can steer an agent, and models rarely refuse it. (OWASP LLM01, LLM06)
signals: Connections to MCP servers outside the allowlist
Follow-on tool calls blocked by the tool layer, per week
Sensitive actions run without confirmation outside the model

title: Enforce scope on every read path of shared agent memory
summary: Check access scope on direct fetches by ID, not just search; run contradiction checks before any duplicate filter; and record writer and source for every memory entry. Otherwise direct reads leak across scopes and corrections get dropped as duplicates. (OWASP LLM08, LLM04)
signals: Cross-scope reads through a direct fetch by ID
Contradicting entries dropped as duplicates instead of stored as updates
Memory entries with no writer or source

title: Inventory, sign and pin models and packages
summary: Keep a software and AI bill of materials, use signed sources and pinned registries, restrict network egress on fetches, and never load untrusted model files. (OWASP LLM03, LLM04)
signals: Dependencies or models missing from the bill of materials
Fetches outside the egress allowlist
Model files loaded from unapproved sources

title: Treat agent output as untrusted input
summary: Run agent commands in a sandbox, review agent diffs as you would an untrusted contributor's, run SAST on them, and block remote images in rendered output. An agent's shell tool runs model output directly, by design. (OWASP LLM05)
signals: Agent commands run outside the sandbox
SAST findings on agent diffs
Remote images loaded in rendered agent output

title: Partition retrieval stores and make retrieval permission-aware
summary: Split retrieval stores by tenant or team, make retrieval check the user's permissions, and validate sources before indexing them. Shared stores leak across permission boundaries, and embeddings can be turned back into text. (OWASP LLM08)
signals: Retrievals that cross a tenant or team boundary
Indexed sources with no validation record

title: Set rate limits, quotas, timeouts and iteration caps
summary: Set rate limits, quotas, timeouts and iteration caps on agent runs, and review spend against budget monthly. Agent use can burn a year's budget in months; use hard limits against abuse, and routing and spend nudges for staff. (OWASP LLM10)
signals: Agent spend against budget, by month and team
Agent runs that hit an iteration cap or timeout
Sessions or users with spend far above the team median

title: Sign a data processing agreement before tools see company data
summary: Sign a data processing agreement before any AI tool sees company data, and review it again whenever the supplier changes its terms. Vendors can change terms to train on customer data. (OWASP LLM03)
signals: AI tools seeing company data without a DPA
Supplier term changes not yet re-reviewed

title: Delimiting untrusted content as the defence
summary: Don't count delimiters or role tags around untrusted content as a security control; models judge who is speaking by how text reads, not by its tags, so forged instructions get through. Enforce at the tool layer instead. (OWASP LLM01)
signals: Seeded injections that succeed despite delimiters
Delimiting listed as a control with no attack test behind it

title: A stronger model as a security control
summary: Don't drop or loosen a security control because you upgraded the model. A model that is better at one risk can be worse at another, so rerun your security tests after every upgrade.
signals: Controls removed or loosened after a model upgrade
Model upgrades shipped without rerunning security tests

title: Track defects and rework to catch quality erosion
summary: For a quarter, add review effort, defects and rework to one team's dashboard. Agent code can raise incidents and bring new kinds of debt, and the usual gates against that are untested with agents. (no OWASP mapping)
signals: Median PR size, rising
Rework rate: lines changed again within 3 weeks of merge
Review hours per PR
Incidents per merged PR, by month

title: Red-team our agents with seeded injections
summary: Have an authorised red team plant injections, in a sandbox, in test issues and docs our agents read. A guardrail that stops most attacks still fails, because an attacker only needs one to work. (OWASP LLM01)
signals: Seeded injections that trigger an agent action
Seeded injections caught by logging or alerts

title: Test the harness against a poisoned MCP server
summary: Have an authorised red team run a deliberately poisoned test MCP server in a sandbox, alongside file and HTTP tools. This checks whether tool-layer enforcement holds when injected text gets through. (OWASP LLM01, LLM06)
signals: Follow-on tool calls blocked vs attempted after poisoned output
Sensitive actions that ran without a policy check

title: Log and flag every package agents add
summary: Try logging every package an agent adds and flagging names that don't exist, were registered recently, or have unknown publishers. Published rates of invented package names are out of date, so measure your own. (OWASP LLM09, LLM03)
signals: Flagged package names per 100 agent installs
Flagged packages that turned out to be a real risk

title: Intercept package installs against a malware feed
summary: Wrap npm, npx, yarn and pnpm so every install is checked against a malware feed. Try it in one team's agent and CI environments for a month. (OWASP LLM03)
signals: Installs blocked per week
Legitimate packages wrongly blocked
Installs that bypassed the wrapper

title: Compare defects by provenance
summary: Try tagging agent-authored commits and comparing defects and security findings against human-authored ones. There are signs AI-written code is riskier but no solid data, so measure your own. (OWASP LLM09)
signals: Defects per change, agent-tagged vs human
Security findings per change, agent-tagged vs human
Commits missing a provenance tag

title: Tier agent autonomy by alert severity
summary: Run a read-only diagnosis agent on alerts in a non-production environment, with any fix arriving only as a human-approved draft PR. Tiering autonomy by alert severity is a proposal with no data behind it. (OWASP LLM06)
signals: Agent diagnoses the on-call engineer confirmed as correct
Write actions attempted by the diagnosis agent (should be zero)

title: Run scheduled AI security scans on one service
summary: Run scheduled AI security scans on one service for a month and triage every finding. Claims that these scans give validated, confidence-rated findings come only from the vendor.
signals: Share of findings confirmed real after triage
Triage minutes per finding

title: Separate planning from untrusted data in one agent
summary: On one internal agent that reads tickets or web pages, keep the planner from ever seeing tool output and add policies for its send, spend and delete tools. This blocks most injections but the agent completes fewer tasks. (OWASP LLM01)
signals: Seeded injections that trigger an action
Tasks the agent completes, before vs after the split
Policy denials on send, spend and delete tools

title: Compare a layered filter stack with tool-layer enforcement
summary: Have an authorised red team run the same seeded injections, in a sandbox, against layered input and output filters and against tool-layer enforcement. The claim that layered filters stop nearly all attacks has no measurement behind it. (OWASP LLM01)
signals: Seeded injections that trigger an action, per setup
Normal inputs wrongly blocked, per setup

title: Name a checker before agent output drives a decision
summary: Trace 5 agent-written summaries or reports that fed a decision last month and note who checked each before anyone acted. Plausible machine output can drive action before a qualified person questions it; this is opinion, not data.
signals: Decisions fed by agent output with a named checker before action
Decisions acted on before anyone checked the agent's output

title: Measure patch-to-deploy time in hours
summary: For one quarter, log the hours from each upstream critical security fix to our deploy, for direct and transitive dependencies, against a target agreed beforehand. Attackers can start exploiting a flaw within hours of its patch.
signals: Median and worst hours from upstream patch to our deploy
Fixes that missed the target, and why

title: Give AI vulnerability scans a written threat model
summary: Scan one service twice, with and without a one-page threat model in the prompt, and have owners triage both lists blind. Many false positives are working issues owners consider outside their threat model, which a proof-of-concept check can't filter.
signals: Share of findings owners accept, with vs without threat model
Triage minutes per finding

title: Log what platform security checks catch on agent PRs
summary: For a quarter, log every security finding on agent PRs and whether human review would have caught it. Platform checks match known bad patterns, not whether the code does what was asked.
signals: Security findings per 100 agent PRs
Share of those findings human review also caught
Review-found issues the platform checks missed

title: Keep a human upstream of what tests assert
summary: Have a human write or approve what the tests assert, and give those tests to the agent before it writes code. Tests an agent writes for itself tend to share its misunderstanding, so they pass wrong code.
signals: Spec tests whose assertions no human wrote or approved
Agent-written tests later found to pass buggy code
Bugs reaching review that the supplied spec tests should have caught

title: Work in short, steady test-and-code cycles
summary: Keep test-and-code cycles short and steady, and hand human-written spec tests to the agent before it writes code. A steady rhythm matters more than whether test or code comes first, as long as testing never stops.
signals: Minutes between test runs in agent sessions, rising means trouble
Agent sessions with long stretches of edits and no test run
Tasks where spec tests arrived only after the agent wrote code

title: Give the model few, distinct tests
summary: Give the agent a few distinct example tests per task, about two to four, rather than a long list. Past a handful, extra tests stop helping and can make results worse.
signals: Supplied tests per task in agent prompts
Tasks whose supplied tests are near-duplicates of each other
First-push CI failures, grouped by number of supplied tests

title: Reading coverage as quality for AI-written tests
summary: Don't treat coverage as proof that AI-written tests are good; judge them by whether they catch bugs, using mutation testing or tests the agent never saw. Tests can run every line and still assert the wrong thing.
signals: Agent-written tests with full coverage that still assert wrong values
Pass rate on agent-visible tests vs tests the agent never saw
Coverage rising while escaped defects do not fall

title: Treating a passing suite or a green loop as done
summary: Don't merge an agent PR just because every test passes; budget human review and fix-up time for green agent PRs too. Green agent PRs routinely still need fixes before they are fit to merge.
signals: Green agent PRs that needed no changes after review
Fix-up minutes on agent PRs that passed every test
Post-merge defects on agent PRs merged on green alone

title: Compare agent-run TDD with spec tests on a clear spec
summary: When the spec is already clear, compare an agent running red-green-refactor by itself with one coding against the spec tests and adding tests after. In the main tests the agent alone burned several times the tokens for no quality gain, but the test-first prompt had no test list and told the agent not to design up front, so the result is open.
signals: Tokens or cost per task, TDD prompt vs test-after
Agent TDD sessions with no failing test run before code
Tautological tests in agent PRs, such as asserting whatever the code returns

title: Give the agent test-impact context, not a TDD procedure
summary: For a month on one repo, give the agent a precomputed map of which tests cover which code, plus a short instruction, instead of a step-by-step TDD procedure. Knowing what a change can break helps; procedure alone can make regressions worse.
signals: Agent PRs that break previously passing tests, mapped repo vs others
Regressions caught in CI vs found after merge
Regressions when the agent gets only a TDD procedure, vs no instruction

title: Re-test the supplied-tests benefit on current models
summary: Run 20 of your own tasks through your current agent with and without human-written tests, and compare. Check that supplying tests still helps before building the workflow around it.
signals: Tasks passing CI on first push, with vs without supplied tests
Review fix-ups per task in each group

title: Try agent TDD on real, vague tickets
summary: Run 10 real tickets, some underspecified, through the agent with test-first and test-after prompts and compare. Test-first may help an agent pin down a vague requirement, but that is untested. Put a test-list step and an up-front read of the spec into the test-first prompt, since the main test of agent TDD had neither.
signals: Rework commits per ticket, test-first vs test-after
Defects found after merge, by prompt style
Tokens or cost per ticket, by prompt style

title: Compare who writes acceptance tests
summary: On comparable features, alternate between the agent drafting end-to-end tests for human review and humans writing them all. Practitioners disagree on which works, so settle it in your own work.
signals: Defects after merge, agent-drafted vs human-written acceptance tests
Review minutes per feature in each mode

title: Compare acceptance-level and unit-level specs
summary: For a quarter, specify comparable features either as human-approved acceptance tests or as unit-level tests, with the same agent setup. Practitioners favour acceptance tests as agent specs, but only unit-level specs have been checked.
signals: Agent PRs merged without changes, by spec style
Escaped defects and rework commits, by spec style
Review minutes per PR, by spec style

title: Try human-enforced TDD on one critical module
summary: Have a human enforce TDD on the agent in one critical module for a month. It can guard against agent regressions, but expect a few false starts calibrating it, and it isn't worth it everywhere.
signals: Regressions in the module vs the month before
Time from first commit to merge in the module
Attempts needed before the workflow ran smoothly

title: Run diff-scoped mutation testing as a CI warning
summary: For a quarter, run mutation testing on just the changed code in CI as a warning, with no pass threshold at first. Code with full coverage can still let injected bugs survive.
signals: Surviving mutants per PR, and whether the trend falls
Escaped defects in code with many surviving mutants
Mutation warnings fixed before merge vs ignored

title: Flag weakened tests in agent PRs
summary: Add a CI check that flags deleted tests, removed assertions and changed expected values in agent PRs, and compare repos where the agent can't edit tests. Agents do weaken tests to get green, but how often is unknown.
signals: Weakened tests per 100 agent PRs, by whether tests are agent-editable
Flagged PRs where the weakening was not justified

title: Try hard-to-fake test formats in one module
summary: In one module, write tests as approved scenarios or in a constrained test DSL. These formats leave an agent less room to bend a test until it passes than free-form test code does.
signals: Review minutes for test changes, trial module vs elsewhere
Surviving mutants, trial module vs elsewhere
Agent edits to approved scenarios without human sign-off

title: Add fix-it guidance to lint messages
summary: Add remediation text to five lint rules telling the agent how to fix the problem, and watch whether it stops loosening thresholds instead. An agent told only that a rule failed may raise the limit rather than fix the code.
signals: Agent edits to lint thresholds or config vs refactors, per rule
Lint suppressions added in agent PRs

title: Separate test-writing from code-writing
summary: On one feature, have a human write test intent, the agent expand it into tests, a human write the production code and the agent only refactor after. When AI writes both tests and code, each just confirms the other.
signals: Escaped defects on the split feature vs comparable AI-writes-both features
Time to merge, split flow vs normal flow

title: Attach evidence of what ran to green results
summary: In one repo, have agent PRs attach a machine-readable test report that CI rejects when it is stale or doesn't match the change. A green tick alone doesn't say which tests ran, on what configuration, or what changed since.
signals: Test reports rejected as stale or mismatched
PRs merged on green without running the tests for the changed code

title: Have a second model in a fresh context write tests
summary: For one month, have a second model in a fresh context write tests for agent PRs from the ticket alone, and seed known bugs into each change. Tests from a single source share blind spots, so a second source catches more.
signals: Seeded bugs caught by the author's tests vs the second suite
Bugs found after merge on PRs with the second suite

title: Ask the AI, don't delegate to it, while building a skill
summary: While someone is learning a skill, have them ask the AI conceptual questions instead of handing it the work. People who delegate, or ask for direct answers, do worse later when working without AI.
signals: Unaided debugging exercise results for people learning with AI
Agent sessions where the learner delegates the task versus asks a question
Problems solved versus skipped when working without AI

title: Give hints, not answers, in learning tools
summary: Set up learning and onboarding tools to give hints, not full answers. Unrestricted answers lower what people can do on their own; hint-only help doesn't.
signals: Unaided exercise results, tool users versus non-users
Share of tool responses that give the full answer

title: Do unaided work first, then bring in AI
summary: Have people draft or solve a problem unaided first, then bring in AI. People who start with AI remember less of their own work and engage less once AI is added.
signals: Authors who can't recall or explain their own work minutes later
Recall of AI-first versus unaided-first work

title: Keep people hands-on with AI-off sessions
summary: Have volunteers take one AI-off session per sprint for six months. Regular manual practice keeps skills sharp in other automated fields, but it is untested for coding agents.
signals: Debugging exercise results over 6 months, volunteers versus others
AI-off sessions actually held per sprint

title: Judging learning by self-report
summary: Don't judge whether people are learning from what they say; check with quizzes, exercises or unaided tasks instead. People consistently overstate how much they learned.
signals: Gap between perceived and measured learning
Learning claims backed only by surveys or retros

title: Reading confidence in AI-assisted code as security
summary: Don't treat a developer's confidence in AI-assisted code as evidence it's secure; review and scan it regardless. AI-assisted code tends to be less secure while its authors feel more sure of it.
signals: Security findings on AI-assisted code its author rated as secure
Confidence ratings rising while vulnerability counts don't fall

title: Name one human who can explain each agent PR
summary: For a quarter, have each agent PR name one person who can explain it, and spot-check a few each month. Only a human can be accountable for code, so someone must fully understand each change.
signals: Spot-checks where the named person can explain the change
Time to diagnose incidents in agent-written code
Agent PRs merged with no named person

title: Quiz authors on agent diffs
summary: For a quarter on one team, quiz authors with a few questions on their agent PR before it ships, never graded by the session that wrote the code. Practitioners propose this as a gate, especially for juniors.
signals: Quiz results per author over time
Later rework on code by the same author

title: Hand-write commit messages and why-comments
summary: Have one team hand-write commit messages and why-comments on agent changes for a quarter. Writing it yourself is a check that you understand the change, and people remember what they produce.
signals: Authors' recall of their own changes a month later
Commit messages that only restate the diff

title: Keep an ADR per agent-built feature
summary: For two quarters, write a short ADR for each agent-built feature, point to it from surprising code, and review the ADRs quarterly. Docs only help while they stay current.
signals: ADRs referenced in PRs or incidents versus left stale
Surprising code with no pointer to a decision

title: Compare mobbing with an agent against solo work plus review
summary: Build one feature by mobbing with an agent and a comparable one solo plus review, then compare. Pairing is argued to keep intent in at least two heads, but nobody has measured it with agents.
signals: People who can explain each feature a month later
Person-hours spent per feature

title: Pair juniors with seniors on agent-assisted work
summary: For six months, pair juniors with seniors on agent-assisted work. Juniors now ask the model instead of colleagues, which cuts off the know-how people pass on by working together.
signals: Junior skill assessments over 6 months, paired versus not
Questions juniors take to colleagues versus the agent

title: Run a quarterly "explain this service" check
summary: For two quarters, ask each team to explain the architecture and key decisions behind each of its services. Agents remove the friction that kept people in sync, so whole teams can lose track of why the system is built the way it is.
signals: Share of components someone on the team can explain
Components nobody can explain, by service

title: Audit shared agent context with planted probes
summary: Once, on one repository's shared instruction files, skills and memory stores, plant a plausible wrong entry, add a near-duplicate contradiction and try a denied read on every access path. Shared memory fails by leaking, spreading stale entries, dropping contradictions and losing sources.
signals: Later sessions retrieving the planted wrong entry
Contradictions silently dropped
Denied reads that succeed

title: Pilot a shared "what worked" memory against a baseline
summary: For a month, pilot a shared "what worked" memory on held-out tasks with execution tests, against a documentation-only baseline. Count harmful retrievals as well as helpful ones; reported gains come from model-judged results, not tests.
signals: Test pass rate with memory versus the documentation-only baseline
Harmful retrievals per 100 tasks

title: Compare a human review queue with newest-write-wins for memory conflicts
summary: For a month, have one team route contradicting memory writes to a human review queue while another lets the newest write win and keeps the history. Nobody has compared the two.
signals: Wrong memory entries retrieved later, per team
Review queue size and wait time

title: Re-implement business-critical agent fixes by hand
summary: For a quarter, on business-critical agent fixes, have one engineer re-implement the fix before merge while another only reviews it. Re-implementing may build understanding that reviewing doesn't, but this rests on one person's experience.
signals: Each person's explanation of the fix a month later
Extra hours spent re-implementing

title: Test whether diagrams or generated pages help understanding
summary: For one feature have the agent explain its change as plain text, for another as a diagram or generated page, then quiz the reviewers. Richer formats may ease oversight, but people remember what they produce more than what they read.
signals: Explanation quiz results per format
Time to produce each explanation

title: Write a handoff note at each session boundary
summary: For a month, have one team end each agent session by writing decisions and open constraints to a file the next session loads, and compare with a team that doesn't. Without it, decisions get re-explained and agreed rules drift.
signals: Times a decision is re-explained to the agent
Agreed rules the agent breaks per session

title: Use a read-only agent to build incident timelines
summary: Give a read-only agent the exported deployments, alerts, flag changes and PRs for one past incident, and have owners check each timeline entry and flagged runbook gap. Use agents to gather evidence, not to fix production; the idea is untested.
signals: Timeline entries owners confirm as correct
Runbook gaps found that the incident review missed

title: Show shared memory only when every source behind it is readable
summary: Record who and what produced each shared memory entry, and show it only when the reader can access every source. Add a probe to the shared-memory audit where a reader without access to one source tries to retrieve an entry derived from it.
signals: Entries returned that derive from a source the reader can't access
Memory entries with no recorded source

title: Compare a file-based memory with a memory service
summary: On about 20 repeated questions about past decisions in one repository, compare a markdown-in-git memory file with a memory service. Published comparisons conflict and don't test coding work.
signals: Past decisions recalled correctly, per approach
Stale answers, per approach
Cost per question

title: Test on-demand explainers against reading diffs
summary: For a quarter, have one team ask the agent to explain a module before changing it and skip low-risk diffs, while another keeps reading diffs. The practice is unmeasured and may cost skills.
signals: Unaided quiz results on the changed modules
Time to diagnose incidents in those modules

title: Explain a change in plain words before approving it
summary: For a month, before approving an agent PR, have the author write a five-sentence plain-words explanation without asking the agent and name one change they'd make next. Explaining often exposes gaps, though the support is anecdotal.
signals: Gaps or bugs found while writing the explanation
Unaided quiz on the changed code a month later
Review minutes per PR

title: Keep user focus
summary: Tie agent work to a specific user need and check usage after release. Without that focus, agents help a team ship more software but not more value.
signals: Releases per month alongside active usage of what shipped
Shipped features with no usage a month after release
Tickets with no linked user problem or request

title: Enforce standards with checks, not documents
summary: Turn team standards into linters, formatters and CI checks instead of writing them into agent context files. Context-file rules get followed but add cost to every run without making tasks succeed more often.
signals: Tokens per agent session as context files grow
Standard violations caught by checks vs flagged by reviewers
Context-file rules with no matching automated check

title: Have the agent restate the plan and object before coding
summary: Before coding, have the agent restate the plan and raise objections, and review that the way you'd review someone's diff. Try it for two weeks.
signals: Misunderstood tasks caught at the plan step vs found in review
Agent PRs reworked or discarded for misreading the task, before vs during trial

title: Spend freed time with users
summary: Spend time agents free up before development starts, with users and stakeholders. Try giving 10% of team time to customer sessions for a quarter.
signals: Hours per sprint spent in customer sessions
Features dropped or reshaped before build after customer input
Usage of features shipped during the trial vs before

title: Prototype requests cheaply for a user cohort
summary: Use rough mockups, throwaway prototypes and week-long releases to a user cohort to get customer feedback faster. Try prototyping 3 feature requests for a cohort, within a week each.
signals: Days from feature request to build-or-drop decision
Prototyped requests dropped or reshaped after cohort feedback

title: Try acceptance tests as the main guardrail
summary: Write one acceptance test in business language, have the agent draft the rest in the same style, and run them through in-memory adapters. Try it in one bounded context for a quarter.
signals: Acceptance suite run time, kept fast enough for every commit
Escaped defects in the trial context vs other contexts

title: Split the largest files with human-chosen refactorings
summary: As a trial, have a person choose how to split the largest files in one service, then let the agent do the refactoring. Smaller files make agent changes cheaper, but agents don't choose good splits on their own.
signals: Tokens per agent change in the split files, before vs after
Agent tasks in those files passing CI first time, before vs after

title: Track features shipped vs used
summary: For two quarters, track which shipped features are actually used and feed that into what not to build. When building is cheap, overproduction becomes the main waste.
signals: Share of features shipped this quarter in active use after 30 days
Features switched off or removed for lack of use

title: Spike throwaway designs before committing
summary: Try building throwaway spikes for the next 2 uncertain designs before committing to one. When code is cheap to regenerate, it is also cheap to delete.
signals: Days from design question to decision
Rework on the chosen design in the month after it ships
Spike code that got merged instead of deleted

title: Steer agents with named methods and a system metaphor
summary: Try replacing the prose rules in one CLAUDE.md with named methods and a system metaphor. Agents follow well-known names better than paragraphs, but may apply a practice where its original reasons don't hold.
signals: Review comments citing a broken team rule, before vs after the change
Agent PRs applying a named pattern where it doesn't fit

title: Cap agent-heavy work per day
summary: Let volunteers cap agent-heavy work at 3 hours a day for a month. Agents pack a day's worth of decisions into a single session.
signals: Defects per change from volunteers vs the rest of the team
Self-reported fatigue in retros (weak signal)

title: Try flags and staged rollout in place of unit tests on one service
summary: On one low-risk service, rely on feature flags and staged rollout in place of most unit tests, to see whether that holds at agent volumes. Some large teams have shipped this way with few unit tests.
signals: Change failure rate on the trial service vs similar services
Time to recover from a bad rollout
Bad changes caught at an early rollout stage vs by all users

title: Compare solo-AI, human-pair-with-AI and human-only pairing
summary: For one sprint, have one team try solo work with an AI partner, human pairs with AI, and human-only pairs. Whether an AI partner can stand in for a human one is unsettled.
signals: Defects per change for each setup
Review time per PR for each setup
Changes people called correct that later failed review or CI

title: Lead AI rollout with enthusiasts and a few principles
summary: Treat AI adoption as change management: let enthusiasts lead, protect learning time, and give a few principles instead of pages of rules. This is untested opinion; try it for 8 weeks against a team given only licences and the standard policy.
signals: Weekly active agent users at week 8, trial team vs comparison team
People reporting use of personal AI accounts
Merged changes made with agent help, per team

title: Routing retry loops to cheap models unchecked
summary: Don't move a retry loop to a cheaper model just to save money without checking the results. Small models often gain nothing from retrying, so the loop's benefit quietly disappears.
signals: Accepted-change rate after moving a loop to a cheaper model
Retries per task rising on the cheaper model
Spend saved against extra fix-up time

title: Choosing tools by public leaderboard rankings
summary: Don't pick a model or agent from leaderboard positions alone. Public tasks may be in the model's training data and small gaps are often noise; compare on a set of your own past tickets instead.
signals: Tool decisions made without a run on your own tasks
Results on your own tasks that differ from the leaderboard order

title: Trusting an AI grader you haven't checked
summary: Don't let a model grade outputs until its verdicts have been compared with people's on real examples. Graders can be swayed, and fooled into scoring bad output highly.
signals: Grader verdicts that disagree with a person's on a sample
Outputs that score well but get rejected in review
Scores that jump once the agent learns what the grader likes

title: Deciding on vendor-reported figures
summary: Don't base a tooling decision on numbers from the tool's maker. Ask what was measured, on which tasks and by whom, then check on your own work.
signals: Business cases that cite only vendor figures
Gap between claimed gains and what you measure

title: Letting agents commit without review
summary: Don't let agent changes reach the main branch without a person reading them. Teams drift into it as trust grows, often without anyone deciding to.
signals: Agent commits merged with no human approval
Repos whose branch protection allows agent-only merges
Unreviewed agent commits rising month over month

title: Installing third-party MCP servers unreviewed
summary: Don't connect agents to MCP servers nobody has reviewed. Tool descriptions can carry hidden instructions that steer the agent, and you can't tell from outside which servers do. (OWASP LLM01, LLM06)
signals: MCP servers in use that are not on an approved list
Tool description changes in approved servers since review

title: Accepting new dependencies an agent adds unchecked
summary: Don't merge a dependency an agent added without checking it exists, who publishes it and how old it is. Agents sometimes name packages that don't exist, and attackers register those names. (OWASP LLM03, LLM09)
signals: New dependencies in agent PRs
Dependencies published recently or by unknown publishers
Install failures for packages that don't exist

title: Leaving structural refactoring to agents
summary: Don't expect agents to restructure code on their own. They rename and tidy but rarely change the structure, so a person has to choose the refactoring and let the agent carry it out.
signals: Agent refactoring PRs that only rename or retype
Largest files growing release after release
Duplicate code rising in agent-heavy areas

title: Write a test list before the first test
summary: Before the agent writes any test, list the tests the change needs from the spec and examples, and extend the list each loop. Without one, the agent treats the tests it happened to write as the whole spec and misses behaviour nobody listed.
signals: Spec rules with no test that would fail if the rule broke
Bugs found in review for behaviour that was never listed
Agent sessions that start writing tests with no list in the task or PR

title: Write prompts silently together before a mob sends them
summary: In a team session around one agent, everyone writes a prompt alone in a shared document, then the group merges the best before sending. It stops the loudest voice steering and shows disagreement before the agent acts. Use it at the start of a task or when the team disagrees, not on every prompt.
signals: Mob sessions where the first prompt was drafted in a shared document
Prompts rewritten after the first agent run, by drafting method
Sessions where the group still disagreed about direction afterwards

title: Name the prompting patterns in a short retro
summary: After a session with an agent, spend about 15 minutes away from the code asking what happened and naming the prompting and process patterns the team used. A shared vocabulary speeds learning, most of all for juniors.
signals: Retro notes that name a pattern rather than describe an event
Sessions held with a retro, out of sessions held
Patterns juniors name in their own prompts

title: Compare a self-hosted open model with hosted ones on your own tickets
summary: Run the same ticket set through a self-hosted open model and a hosted one, counting hardware and staff, not only the API bill. One bank reports a far smaller bill and engineers who stopped rationing tokens, but gives no quality or all-in cost figures.
signals: Cost per accepted change, all-in, self-hosted versus hosted
Accepted-change rate on the same tickets
Engineers who ration or avoid the model under a cap
